---
title: "Get started with zujose"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

zujose signs, verifies, encrypts and decrypts JOSE objects. This article
walks through the pieces in the order you meet them: keys, JSON Web Tokens,
signatures and encryption underneath, and reading a token you have not
checked yet.

```{r, message = FALSE}
library(zujose)
```

## The vocabulary

JOSE (JSON Object Signing and Encryption) is a family of standards:

* a **JWS** (RFC 7515) is a signed payload;
* a **JWE** (RFC 7516) is an encrypted payload;
* a **JWK** (RFC 7517) is a key written as JSON, and a JWK Set is a list
  of them;
* a **JWT** (RFC 7519) is a set of claims, such as who the token is about
  and when it expires, carried as the payload of a JWS or a JWE.

Each comes in a *compact* serialization, the familiar
`xxxxx.yyyyy.zzzzz`, and a JSON one. RFC 7518 lists the algorithms. Every
function in zujose starts with `jose_`; the token or payload is the first
argument and the key the second.

## Keys

A key is a `jose_key`. A symmetric key, of type `oct`, is a secret shared
by whoever signs and whoever verifies. Generate one for the algorithm you
mean to use, and it is the right length:

```{r}
hmac <- jose_key_generate("oct", alg = "HS256", kid = "hmac-1")
hmac
```

Printing never shows the secret. An existing secret, as raw bytes, is
wrapped with `jose_key_oct()`. A password is not a key: turn it into one
with a key derivation function, or use PBES2 encryption, which does that
for you.

Public-key algorithms need a key pair. zujose makes RSA keys and
elliptic-curve keys on P-256, P-384, P-521 and X25519:

```{r}
signer <- jose_key_generate("EC", crv = "P-256", alg = "ES256", kid = "ec-1")
signer
```

`as_jose_key()` reads a key from JWK text or from PEM, and `jose_jwk()` and
`jose_pem()` write one. Both write only the public part unless you ask for
the private one:

```{r}
jose_jwk(signer)
```

A key set holds several keys. Its JWK Set text is what an identity
provider publishes, and what a client reads to verify the provider's
tokens:

```{r}
keys <- jose_keyset(signer, jose_key_generate("RSA", alg = "RS256", kid = "rsa-1"))
keys
cat(jose_jwk(keys))
```

`as_jose_keyset()` reads that text back. A key in a set is picked by the
`kid` in a token's header. Two more tools help with naming keys:
`jose_with_kid()` names a key by its RFC 7638 thumbprint, which needs no
registry, and `jose_thumbprint()` computes the thumbprint itself.

Keys live in ordinary R memory, which R can copy and cannot wipe. See the
"Secrets in memory" section of `?jose_key_oct` for what that means.

## JSON Web Tokens

`jose_jwt_encode()` signs a list of claims. `expires_in` sets `exp`, and
`iat` is added for you:

```{r}
jwt <- jose_jwt_encode(
  list(iss = "https://auth.example", sub = "user-17", aud = "orders-api"),
  signer,
  expires_in = 600
)
```

`jose_jwt_decode()` checks the token in one call. You say which algorithms
you accept; there is no default, so a token cannot choose a weaker one for
you. The key must fit the algorithm. Then the claims are checked: `exp` is
required by default, `nbf` and `iat` are checked when present, with a
leeway of 60 seconds, and `audience`, `issuer` and `subject` are matched
when you give them:

```{r}
claims <- jose_jwt_decode(
  jwt,
  jose_public(signer),
  algorithms = "ES256",
  audience = "orders-api",
  issuer = "https://auth.example"
)
claims
```

`claims` takes per-claim expectations, as a value or as a function that
must return `TRUE`, and `validate` takes one function of all the claims:

```{r}
jose_jwt_decode(
  jwt,
  jose_public(signer),
  algorithms = "ES256",
  audience = "orders-api",
  claims = list(sub = function(sub) startsWith(sub, "user-"))
)$sub
```

When the same checks apply to every request, `jose_jwt_decoder()` fixes
them once and returns a function of the token:

```{r}
check <- jose_jwt_decoder(
  key = jose_public(keys),
  algorithms = c("ES256", "RS256"),
  audience = "orders-api",
  issuer = "https://auth.example"
)
check(jwt)$sub
```

## When a check fails

Every error is a condition whose class says what failed, all inheriting
from `zujose_error`. Catch the class, not the message:

```{r}
expired <- jose_jwt_encode(list(sub = "user-17"), hmac, expires_in = -3600)
tryCatch(
  jose_jwt_decode(expired, hmac, algorithms = "HS256"),
  zujose_expired_error = function(e) paste("expired at", e$time)
)
```

A token signed with an algorithm you did not allow is a policy error,
raised before any cryptography is done:

```{r, error = TRUE}
jose_jwt_decode(jwt, jose_public(signer), algorithms = "RS256")
```

`?zujose_error` lists every class and the fields each carries.

## Signatures: JWS

A JWT is a JWS whose payload is a JSON object. `jose_sign()` and
`jose_verify()` sign and verify any payload, given as a string or as raw
bytes:

```{r}
token <- jose_sign("Order 1042 shipped.", hmac)
verified <- jose_verify(token, hmac, algorithms = "HS256")
rawToChar(verified$payload)
```

`format = "flattened"` or `"general"` writes the JSON serialization, and
several signers, made with `jose_signer()`, sign one payload together:

```{r}
token <- jose_sign(
  "Order 1042 shipped.",
  list(jose_signer(hmac), jose_signer(signer)),
  format = "general"
)
```

By default every signature must verify. A recipient that holds only one of
the keys asks for any one signature instead:

```{r}
jose_verify(
  token,
  jose_public(signer),
  algorithms = "ES256",
  require = "any"
)$kid
```

## Encryption: JWE

A JWE is encrypted in two layers: a random content encryption key encrypts
the payload (`enc`), and the key management algorithm (`alg`) delivers
that key to the recipient. To encrypt for a public key, use the
recipient's public key:

```{r}
recipient <- jose_key_generate("RSA", kid = "rsa-enc")
jwe <- jose_encrypt(
  "card ending 4242",
  jose_public(recipient),
  alg = "RSA-OAEP-256",
  enc = "A256GCM"
)
```

Decrypting names both the key management and the content encryption
algorithms you accept:

```{r}
out <- jose_decrypt(
  jwe,
  recipient,
  algorithms = "RSA-OAEP-256",
  encryptions = "A256GCM"
)
rawToChar(out$plaintext)
```

Every decryption failure raises `zujose_decrypt_error` with the same
message, whatever went wrong, so a failure tells an attacker nothing about
the key.

A password encrypts through PBES2, which derives the key from it. Give the
password to `jose_key_oct()` as bytes:

```{r}
password <- jose_key_oct(charToRaw("correct horse battery staple"))
jwe <- jose_encrypt(
  "backup notes",
  password,
  alg = "PBES2-HS256+A128KW",
  enc = "A128GCM"
)
rawToChar(jose_decrypt(jwe, password, "PBES2-HS256+A128KW", "A128GCM")$plaintext)
```

## Encrypted JWTs

A JWT can be signed and then encrypted, so that only the recipient can read
the claims. Compose the two steps:

```{r}
nested <- jose_jwt_encode(list(sub = "user-17"), signer, expires_in = 600) |>
  jose_encrypt(
    jose_public(recipient),
    alg = "RSA-OAEP-256",
    enc = "A256GCM",
    header = list(cty = "JWT")
  )
```

`jose_jwt_decode()` accepts an encrypted JWT only when you say how to
decrypt it, with `jose_decryption()`. Without it, a JWE where a signed
token was expected is refused:

```{r}
jose_jwt_decode(
  nested,
  jose_public(signer),
  algorithms = "ES256",
  decrypt = jose_decryption(recipient, "RSA-OAEP-256", "A256GCM")
)$sub
```

## Reading a token without checking it

Sometimes you need to look inside a token before you can check it, for
example to read its `kid` or `iss` and choose a key. `jose_peek()` decodes
every part of a token and verifies nothing:

```{r}
jose_peek(jwt)
```

Its result is classed `jose_unverified` and says so. Use it to decide which
key or policy to apply, never to decide whether to trust the token.

## Limits and supported algorithms

Every function that reads a token checks its size, its header, the number
of signatures or recipients and the PBES2 iteration count against
`jose_limits()` before decoding anything. The defaults suit ordinary
tokens; raise them only for a source you trust.

`zujose_info()` lists every algorithm and whether the installed zucrypt
provides it:

```{r}
head(zujose_info())
```
